# Preface {.unnumbered}

<div style="display:flex">
<div style="flex:70%;margin-right:1em;">

The target audience for this tutorial is people with no prior experience with Git, version controls systems, or use of command-line interfaces. The aim of the tutorial is to learn how to use Git, but also to understand how Git works, at least on some superficial level, so that you don't end up in the situation depicted in the webcomic. In a further effort to avoid this scenario, we will also focus on using Git exclusively from the command line, instead of using a GUI or a Git integration in a code editor. GUIs and Git integrations can make learning Git a less daunting endeavour, but it also comes with the very real risk of not actually learning much Git. Furthermore, you can use Git from the command-line on any computer, whereas you might not have access to your favourite GUI or code editor on different systems that you need to work on.

</div>
<div style="margin:1em;">

::: {.column-margin}
Webcomic title text:<br>
"If that doesn't fix it, git.txt contains the phone number of a friend of mine who understands git. Just wait through a few minutes of 'It's really pretty simple, just think of branches as...' and eventually you'll learn the commands that will fix everything."
:::

The tutorial is structured in two parts. Part I is an introduction to Git, and goes through all the basic commands while giving some insights into what Git is and how it works along the way. Part II includes stand-alone chapters on more advanced topics. These chapters are not essential to learning how to use Git, and can be read to the extent they are relevant and of interest. Finally, the tutorial includes appendices on miscellaneous topics.

## Prerequisites

This tutorial assumes you are using Git version 2.51.0 or newer. If you are using an older version of Git, some of the `git config` commands in @sec-configuration-of-git might not work, the `git switch` and `git restore` command might not be available, and there might be other unknown issues as well.

It is assumed you are on a Windows machine and have "Git for Windows" installed. See @sec-git-for-windows for details on how to install "Git for Windows". We will be running Git exclusively from the command line using Git Bash, a Bash emulator, so macOS users should be able to follow along with few or no modifications, since the default shell on macOS is Zsh (or Bash on older systems). If you are a Linux user, you should know what you are doing, and have no problem following along no matter what shell you are using.

As stated in the beginning of the preface, this tutorial does not require you to have any prior experience with working from the terminal, interacting with your computer using shell commands. However, this is exclusively what we will be doing in this tutorial, so if this is unknown territory for you, start this tutorial by reading @sec-git-for-windows, which gives an introduction to this subject. We will also use shell commands to create/edits/list files etc. in examples and exercises, since this makes it possible to clearly and concisely describe what and how to do different things. That being said, if you are uncomfortable using shell commands for basic tasks like creating folders, editing files and so forth, it is totally fine to do this manually in however way you want.

Finally, if you want to follow along in @sec-introduction-to-github, you will need to create a GitHub account and authenticate with it, using the GitHub CLI, which you also need to install. See @sec-introduction-to-github for more details on how two do this.
